picks.title: CRISPR/Cas for diatom gene editing: pitfalls, solutions, and emerging tools.
picks.hook: Diatom CRISPR tools reveal pitfalls and new solutions for editing photosynthetic microalgae.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to improve the use of CRISPR/Cas tools for editing the genes of diatoms, a group of single‑cell algae important for biotechnology. The researchers examined the challenges of applying CRISPR/Cas in these organisms and explored possible solutions and new tools.

They reviewed the unique evolutionary background of diatoms, which carry many species‑specific genes whose functions are largely unknown, and considered how CRISPR‑based genome editing could be used to uncover gene roles and add desirable traits.

The work identified several pitfalls in current diatom CRISPR methods, proposed practical ways to overcome them, and highlighted emerging techniques that may enhance editing efficiency and precision.

Understanding and fixing these issues is valuable because it paves the way for more reliable genetic engineering of diatoms, supporting their development as sustainable bio‑production platforms.
picks.why: Better diatom gene editing could boost algae‑based biotech, from biofuels to high‑value compounds.

picks.title: Mn<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> nanozymes scavenge photocatalytic ROS to enhance photosynthetic CO<sub>2</sub> fixation by microalgae-based biohybrid.
picks.hook: Mn3O4 nanozyme shields microalgae from ROS, boosting CO₂ fixation in hybrid systems.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether adding a special nano‑material could protect microalgae from harmful reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated during light‑driven reactions, and thereby boost the algae’s ability to turn CO₂ into biomass.

The researchers mixed a manganese oxide nanozyme, Mn₃O₄, with microalgal cultures. These nanozymes act like antioxidant enzymes, breaking down excess ROS. The work was done at the laboratory scale, using standard algal growth setups.

They found that the Mn₃O₄ nanozymes successfully scavenged the photocatalysis‑induced ROS, relieving oxidative stress and improving photosynthetic activity and growth of the algae.

This is interesting because it shows a way to combine nanomaterials with algae to make bio‑production processes more efficient.
picks.why: Reducing oxidative stress with nanozymes could help algae produce more biofuel or feed with less energy input.

picks.title: Transcriptomic insights into fermented Spirulina-mediated remodelling of lipid homeostasis to alleviate glucose-induced hyperlipidemia.
picks.hook: Fermented Spirulina reshapes lipid genes, easing glucose‑induced hyperlipidemia in mice.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to understand how fermented Spirulina changes the way cells handle fats when blood sugar is high. The researchers grew cells under high‑glucose conditions and treated them with a probiotic‑fermented Spirulina preparation, then examined the cells' gene activity using transcriptomic analysis, which reads the messages (RNA) that tell cells which proteins to make.

The analysis revealed that the fermented Spirulina altered the expression of genes involved in lipid homeostasis, the balance of fat synthesis, storage, and breakdown. These gene changes pointed to a remodeling of lipid metabolism pathways that could counteract the excess fat accumulation typically seen in glucose‑induced hyperlipidemia.

The findings suggest that fermented Spirulina may help rebalance fat metabolism under high‑sugar stress, offering a potential dietary tool to mitigate hyperlipidemia.

This is interesting because it links a functional food ingredient to specific molecular actions that could support heart‑healthy metabolism.
picks.why: Fermented Spirulina may help regulate fat metabolism, offering a natural dietary approach to manage high‑sugar related lipid disorders.

picks.title: Integrating algal-bacterial consortia and Daphnia magna cultivation for aquaculture wastewater treatment: Water polishing, pathogen control, and live feed production.
picks.hook: Algal‑bacterial consortia with Daphnia polish aquaculture waste while producing live feed.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to create a combined treatment system that could clean aquaculture wastewater, keep harmful microbes in check, and produce live feed for fish. The researchers linked a light‑driven algal‑bacterial consortium with the cultivation of the tiny crustacean Daphnia magna, testing the chain in a series of lab‑scale reactors.

They grew three photobio‑reactors, each inoculated with a different mix of microbial species, and then passed the treated water to tanks where Daphnia magna were raised. The setup was designed to polish the water, reduce pathogen levels, and generate biomass that could be harvested as live feed.

The integrated system successfully removed nutrients from the wastewater, lowered pathogen counts, and produced Daphnia biomass suitable for use as aquaculture feed, demonstrating that the combined approach can achieve water polishing, pathogen control, and live‑feed production in one process.

This work shows how coupling algae‑bacterial treatment with small‑animal cultivation could make aquaculture more sustainable by turning waste streams into valuable resources.
picks.why: It turns fish farm waste into clean water and nutritious feed, boosting sustainability.
